CausalChain: Hypoxia -> Activation of HIFs -> Upregulation of PHGDH -> Enhanced serine synthesis and folate cycle -> Increased NADPH production -> Effective ROS detoxification -> Tumor survival and immunosuppressive TME; Dual inhibition (PHGDH + PPP) -> Profound NADPH depletion -> Elevated ROS -> Induction of immunogenic cell death -> Enhanced T cell activation -> Synergy with immune checkpoint inhibition
Hypothesis: In hypoxic HCC cells, we propose that a dual metabolic targeting strategy—combining the selective inhibition of PHGDH with blockade of compensatory NADPH-producing pathways such as the PPP—will lead to a critical collapse in redox homeostasis by markedly reducing overall NADPH levels. This metabolic disruption is predicted to result in an exaggerated accumulation of ROS, thereby triggering immunogenic cell death and releasing damage-associated molecular patterns that recondition the tumor microenvironment to favor antitumor immunity. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as single-cell metabolomic profiling, CRISPR screening, and high-resolution imaging, this approach aims to precisely target tumor cell metabolic dependencies while preserving effector T cell function. The resultant immunogenic cell death is anticipated to synergize with immune checkpoint inhibitors, overcoming resistance mechanisms mediated by HIF signaling, glycolytic reliance, and mitochondrial adaptations.
Abstract: We hypothesize that a dual metabolic intervention strategy—combining selective inhibition of PHGDH with targeted disruption of compensatory NADPH-generating pathways such as the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP)—in hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells will more robustly impair cellular redox homeostasis. Under hypoxic conditions, HIF activation upregulates PHGDH to bolster serine synthesis and the folate cycle, thereby enhancing NADPH production for reactive oxygen species (ROS) detoxification. Our approach leverages advanced single‐cell metabolomics and genome‐wide CRISPR screens to identify metabolic vulnerabilities unique to hypoxic tumor niches. By further integrating state‐of‐the-art imaging and digital pathology tools for real‐time metabolic profiling, this strategy aims to induce profound ROS accumulation that triggers immunogenic cell death, thereby reprogramming the tumor microenvironment and amplifying the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors—all while sparing effector T cell metabolism.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that PHGDH inhibition in hypoxic HCC cells reduces NADPH production, leading to ROS-mediated immunogenic cell death and enhanced checkpoint inhibitor response, while sparing effector T cell metabolism. Our revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain but addresses key concerns by incorporating the inhibition of compensatory pathways (i.e., the PPP) to prevent metabolic bypass and ensure robust NADPH depletion. In addition, we integrate advanced technological approaches—including single-cell metabolomics, CRISPR screening, and cutting-edge imaging—to refine target specificity and therapeutic monitoring. These modifications enhance the practical implementability and novelty of the hypothesis by directly countering potential redundancies in NADPH production and by providing a comprehensive framework to monitor metabolic and immune responses in real time.
